newsitem.title: POLAND: Poland mulls army cuts before joining NATO.
newsitem.headline: Poland mulls army cuts before joining NATO.

text.p: Poland is considering substantial cuts in the number of its troops as part of a programme to upgrade its armed forces to NATO standards before its entry into the alliance, a government minister said on Monday.
"Various options are being considered, including one to considerably reduce the number of personnel in the army," deputy defence minister Andrzej Karkoszka told Reuters in an interview.
Poland now has 233,000 troops, 1,720 tanks and 440 fighting planes and military analysts say the armed forces should become leaner but more flexible and better equipped before NATO entry.

Karkoszka said the priority of the programme, now being discussed in parliament's defence committee, was to adjust the forces to NATO's operational procedures by 1999, when Poland hopes to join the Western military alliance along with some other former members of the defunct Soviet bloc.

"Our goal is to make the Polish armed forces inter-operational with the forces of NATO member countries... regarding communication, command procedures, language, maps and management of air space," he said.

Poland, along with the Czech Republic and Hungary, hopes to be invited to join NATO at its Madrid summit in July and complete accession talks by the end of the year, despite Russia's opposition to the pact's eastward expansion.

Karkoszka said the defence ministry was evaluating the costs of joining NATO. They were hard to define precisely but would be smaller than the costs of modernising the armed forces outside the alliance, he said.
"If we were to modernise our army alone and create a military doctrine for a single country, we would have to spend more and achieve a far poorer defence effect," he said.

He said his ministry's estimates for the cost of NATO expansion were similar to those suggested by a U.S. administration report, due to be presented to Congress on Monday, whose elements were published by the Washington Post.
The paper reported on Sunday that the expansion of NATO would cost more than $30 billion over the next 12 years.

The report also assumed that the new members selected at the Madrid summit would pick up 35 percent of the cost of joining, that current members other than the United States would pay about 50 percent, and that the United States would pay 15 percent.
"According to our calculations, the costs would even be slightly smaller," Karkoszka said.
He said that within several months his ministry should finish work on specifications for a new jet fighter which the Polish air force is preparing to buy.

Defence ministry officials have said Poland needs about 100 multi-task fighters to replace its outmoded Soviet-made MIG 21 jets and effectively protect its air space. U.S. and European firms are lobbying for the contract.
Karkoszka said the scope of the fighter programme, seen as very costly for the meagre Polish defence budget, would be subject to a political decision by parliament.
